rv.q: What it lacks in polish, it more than compensates for in truth, specificity, and urgency.
Just about anyone will find it honest and thoroughly gripping.
Stachel, along with Taccone and dramaturg Madeleine Oldham, have landed on a lean script performed with charm, vulnerability, and moments that push catharsis to the brink of exorcism.
His performance is impressive, brave and deeply unsettling.
His personal struggle to define his identity is just as heartbreaking as it can be frustrating to watch.
He never asks for pity, places blame, or makes excuses, but bravely and honestly reveals his scars, shows us his wounds, and involves us in his process of healing.

But Stachel doesn't provide enough specificity to make his story really come alive, especially since he seems to have escaped without any onstage meltdowns, dire medical interventions, or career-ending episodes.
